story.logline: Wake the canyon's great sky-clock by reading the rhythms its machines run on, before the evening star Vesper sets.

approach.text: The Vesper Dial! It tells the Orrery where the evening star rises. Its carriage is parked at sunrise.
Fog hides the star's lens, so we can't aim by eye. The dial only knows the bearing in radians.

instruction.text: Swing the carriage along the rail to 5π/6 so Vesper's light can find its lens.

tutorial.text: Drag the orange knob or use the arrow keys. Only quarter marks are labelled; count the small studs.

insight.text: Each labelled stud marks a quarter lap, and six small studs split every quarter.

hints.text: A full lap of the rail is 2π, so π is only halfway round. Hoo, that's the whole trick.
5π/6 is a little less than π. Count the studs in sixths of π, starting from sunrise.
It sits between the top mark, π/2, and the halfway mark, π, closer to halfway.

default.text: The beam hit the rim, not the lens. Recount the studs from sunrise.

line.text: The beam hit fog. The carriage stopped short; count the gaps from sunrise again.
Past it! The light's scattering off the rim. Walk the carriage back and recount the sixths.
Five-sixths of the whole rail, and the beam's in the floor. π only walks you halfway round.

success.text: A radian is a walk, not a turn: π carries you exactly halfway round any circle.

payoffLine.text: Vesper's lens! And the dial is turning its spokes into a stair. Up we go!

after.text: One rhythm restored. See that beam climbing to the rim? The Orrery felt it.

approach.text: The Tidewheel Gate. Its ring runs on y = sin(2t). It must lap once and lock, or the canals stay dry.
Those rings spin on a sine wave. Watch how fast, not how far.

instruction.text: Set the latch timer to one full period, so the ring's notch comes home and the gate locks open.

tutorial.text: The ring shows where it'll be when the latch fires. The green ghost is the wave, shifted by your timer.

insight.text: Where the green ghost lies exactly on the white wave, the ring is home and heading the same way.

hints.text: A period is how long the ring takes to come back to where it started, moving the same way.
For y = sin(b·t), one period lasts 2π/|b|. The 2 in sin(2t) is b.

default.text: The pawl found no notch to catch. Watch the ring come home, moving the way it started.

line.text: The latch waited too long: the ring kept going past home and the catch slipped. One lap is all it wants.
Too soon! The notch hasn't come home. A faster wheel still needs one whole lap.
Half a lap: the wave's back at zero, but heading down. A period ends moving the way it began.
Two laps! The tally counts two. The gate wants one lap, not the lap of plain old sin(t).
Two laps! The tally counts two. The gate wants one lap, not the lap of plain old sin(t).

success.text: Speed up the wheel and every lap gets shorter: double b, and the period halves.

payoffLine.text: Hoo-hoo! Listen to that water. The Tidewheel's turning again.

after.text: Two rhythms. Brasswick's arm should be back in step. He's been waiting on that water.

approach.text: The Echo Choir. Three automata sing the builders' laws of amplitude. One is a mimic in a choir shell.
Mimics love a half-truth. Aim the Tuning Lens at a singer and compare its trace to the reference.

instruction.text: Aim the Tuning Lens at each singer, compare its trace to the reference wave, and expose the mimic.

tutorial.text: White is the astronomer's wave; green is the aimed singer's claim. The orange probe walks the lens's playhead.

insight.text: Listen as the probe walks: the bell sings the distance from the middle, peak or trough alike.

hints.text: Amplitude is measured from the midline, not across the whole swing.
Peak to trough is twice the amplitude. Check where each singer starts its bracket.
The mimic claims: The amplitude of y = 3sin(x) is 6, peak to trough.

default.text: An honest bell! That singer's claim holds. Look again at where each bracket starts measuring.

success.text: Amplitude is measured from the middle: swing up to 3 and down to −3, and the amplitude is still 3.

payoffLine.text: Sss! Six looked so much bigger. Nobody measures from the middle anymore...

after.text: It was jamming the lift gear! The Echo Lift is rising. Hop on, Wren.
Three rhythms. The crystals up here are waking. Hear them humming?

approach.text: The Chasm of Two Answers. The span holds only if its stones are laid in the order you'd solve 2sin(x) = 1.
Two anchor pylons on the far side. The Measurers never built two pylons for nothing.

instruction.text: Lay the glyph stones in solving order to build the span. One stone doesn't belong.

tutorial.text: Pick a stone, then a socket. Socket 1 is nearest you. Lay the Span once every socket is filled.

insight.text: The lip relief is carved as 2 sin x, the water line sits at 1, and every glint marks where they meet.

hints.text: Get the sine by itself before anything else.
Find the quadrant-I angle whose sine is 1/2. That's your reference angle.
Sine is positive in two quadrants, which is why there are two answers, and two pylons.

default.text: The span won't hold that way. Watch where it tips: the order breaks right there.

line.text: The span held up to a point, then a stone tipped. Something has to happen right before that one.
That stone crumbled: no angle has a sine of 2. You can't undo the 2 until the sine stands alone.
The span reached for both pylons too soon. It needs one more fact about the circle first.

success.text: An equation can have two doors: sine is positive twice on every lap, at π/6 and at 5π/6.

payoffLine.text: Both pylons lit! Isolate, reference angle, quadrants, both solutions. Now let's walk it.

after.text: Four rhythms. The Crystal Stair is ahead, and I can hear the Treasury chimes.

approach.text: The Chime Treasury. Its singers remember the Tidewheel Gate, and one of them remembers it wrong.
This is the trickiest choir yet. Every claim sounds like something we've already seen.

instruction.text: Aim the lens at each singer, count the cycles inside its period bracket, and expose the mimic.

insight.text: A true period bracket closes exactly where the wave comes home, moving the same way.

hints.text: Period = 2π/|b|. Check each claim with it.
A bigger b means a faster wave and a shorter period. A true period bracket holds exactly one cycle.
The mimic claims: y = sin(2x) has period 4π, twice that of sin(x).

default.text: Honest! That bracket holds exactly one cycle. Test the others with 2π over b.

success.text: A wave that repeats twice as often waits half as long: sin(2x) comes home every π.

payoffLine.text: Twice the b, twice the period... it sounded so fair. Sss.

after.text: The Treasury chest! The Warden's key-stone, and the rim stair's growing. Hoo, up!
Five rhythms. One seal left, and it has a guard.

instruction.text: Tune the counter-pendulum's period to the shield's rhythm, y = 3sin((π/2)t), and hold the sync thread.

tutorial.text: Your pendulum swings with the period you set. When the rhythms match, the thread between them stays bright.

insight.text: The thread stays bright only while the two rhythms agree. It never cares how wide either one swings.

hints.text: The 3 in front sets how far the shield swings, not how fast.
Divide 2π by π/2: the π's cancel.

default.text: Don't let the big swing fool you. Watch one full sweep: out, back, and out again the same way.

success.text: How far a thing swings says nothing about how often. Height is A; timing is b.

payoffLine.text: Your timing is true. Pass, reader of rhythms.

fail.text: Out of step, reader. Watch me once more.

line.text: Too slow! You drift behind my every beat.
Too quick! You race ahead and fall out of step.
You count my reach, not my rhythm. Reach is how far. Rhythm is how often.
Zero, yes, but which way do I swing? Half a beat is no beat at all.

lines.text: Oh! A visitor. Oh dear. My arm swings as far as ever, but it keeps coming back too soon.
The Tidewheel used to set my rhythm. Since it stopped, I water the air. The crystals are disappointed.
Whoever you are: if you hear this, you read the rhythms. Angles, periods, swings and solutions.
Above the canyon, the Orrery once turned the sky's rhythms into light, water and time.
Then the astronomer Ilse Vantor sealed her Star Chart away, and the great machine fell out of step.
Gates froze mid-turn. The Tidewheels stalled. The crystal groves began to fade.
Tonight the evening star Vesper rises, and a courier named Wren has come to answer an old letter.
Hoo! Hoo... oh! Someone wound me. Nobody has wound me in years.
Cog, at your service: assistant to Astronomer Vantor, measurer of arcs, and very good at owling.
Hoo! The astronomer's crypt runs on rhythm. Read the rhythm, and every door will open.
Six rhythm seals hold the Orrery still. Each one we restore sends a beam of starlight up to it.
Her Star Chart waits in the Warden's Dome at the top of the canyon. We need it before Vesper sets.
You can't force brass. You move it in step with the wave it runs on. I'll show you how.
The shield's open and the Star Chart is right there! Take it to the lens, Wren!
Under Vesper's light, the Star Chart slid into the Orrery's lens.
Six rhythms, six beams. Hoo, look at them climb!
Whoever you are: if you hear this, you read the rhythms. Angles, periods, swings and solutions.
I sealed the chart so only someone who understood the machines could restart them. Thank you.
The Tidewheels turned. The canals filled terrace by terrace. The groves glowed blue again.
Her star chart! You read every rhythm in the crypt.
Same time next year? I'll keep the gears oiled. Hoo.
The Warden. It guards the Star Chart and trusts only one thing: timing.
None pass whose timing is false.
My shield sweeps three spans either way. Six spans, end to end! Match THAT, little reader.
